newsitem.title: GERMANY: Damaged dike threatens more floods in east Germany.
newsitem.headline: Damaged dike threatens more floods in east Germany.

text.p: German border authorities said on Wednesday a flood barrier holding back the swollen Oder River near the village of Hohenwutzen had broken and would be impossible to repair immediately.

Officials added it was not clear how much of the dike had actually given way or the amount of water coming through. Officials offered varying accounts of the damage. Some said the dike had burst and others said only part of it had torn away.
Sirens sounded, warning a further 1,000 inhabitants to prepare to evacuate the low-lying Oderbruch area, which officials said earlier could be flooded within hours if the dike at Hohenwutzen broke.
A spokesman for border control authorities in Frankfurt an der Oder said the dike had no longer been able to contain the immense pressure of the river.
"It (the water) is running," said the spokesman, adding that military helicopters were trying to block holes in the dike by dumping sand onto the flood barricades.
The floods hitting Poland and the Czech Republic this month have claimed more than 100 lives. No deaths have been reported in Germany but homes, businesses and farms have been extensively damaged.

Border guards at the scene said the area immediately threatened by the dike break was the northern-most swathe of the Oderbruch, a fertile plain north of Frankfurt an der Oder, where 5,000 of the 19,000 residents were evacuated last week.

Earlier, floods showed signs of receding after a fresh high-water surge expected overnight did not materialise, although officials had said many flood-barriers were extremely porous and riddled with weak spots.

Oderbruch, once the breadbasket of the former communist East Germany, was drained 250 years ago to create fertile farmland and is vulnerable to flooding because it lies lower than the river, which is held back by dikes.
The Oder dikes have not failed since 1947, when floods wrought havoc around the town of Reitwein, north of Frankfurt an der Oder.

The European Union proposed on Wednesday 1.5 million Ecu ($1.6 million) in relief aid for the German state of Brandenburg in order to help the battered region cope with the worst flooding seen in more than 200 years.

EU Regional Affairs Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies told a news conference the European Commission would consult the European Parliament over the proposed aid. It was unclear how quickly the money would be made available.
